newsitem.title: USA: Congress wrestles disaster aid, budget details.
newsitem.headline: Congress wrestles disaster aid, budget details.

text.p: Senate Republican leaders on Tuesday insisted Congress needs special legislation to prevent a government shutdown but Democrats objected to what they said were automatic cuts in spending contained in the bill.
The dispute held up passage of a bill to make emergency disaster relief available to flooded states in the upper Midwest and pay for U.S. military operations overseas.

President Bill Clinton has threatened to veto the $8.4 billion spending bill unless the automatic spending provision is taken out. It would continue government operations at a lower, 98 percent, rate beyond Oct. 1 if Congress and the White House cannot agree on new funding for fiscal year 1998.

Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott told reporters Republicans are committed to passage of the stop-gap spending bill, known as the emergency continuing resolution, but said he would talk to the White House about this issue and others the adminstration does not want passed.

Late Tuesday, Lott took the Senate floor to grouse that the Democrats were holding up the disaster aid bill and complain there were 109 amendments pending. But he also said he was open to resolving the automatic spending issue as part of another bill.
"It doesn't need to be in this bill and it doesn't need to be a specific way," Lott said. He fumed that the bill "is supposed to be an emergency supplemental appropriation."

Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle denied Democrats were holding up the bill, but complained the automatic spending provision would force cuts in domestic programmes -- even as Republicans were agreeing to higher spending levels under a new balanced budget deal.
Democrats and some House Republicans fear it will take away all incentive for finishing the routine spending bills on time.
"If we put Congress on automatic...why do a budget agreement?" Daschle said.

Senate Appropriations Committee chairman Ted Stevens, asked why the anti-shutdown bill was necessary, replied, "Because of the way we were being beaten up and treated over the shutdowns. We didn't think we caused it."

Polls showed the public blamed Republican leaders of Congress for two partial government shutdowns in 1996-97 which saw the Christmas holiday closure of popular national parks, including Arizona's Grand Canyon.

Meanwhile, Democratic lawmakers pressed for more details on the budget agreement with the White House. House Minority Leader Richard Gephardt, a Missouri Democrat, said the big question was who would win on taxes.
"There is more we don't know than we do know about the tax package that the Republicans intend to put forth," Gephardt said in a letter to Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin.
Senate Budget Committee chairman Pete Domenici predicted the budget, which is really a blueprint for future action on taxes and spending, will pass easily.
Both Republicans and Clinton's minority Democrats signed on to the plan to balance the balance by 2002 and craft a net $85 billion tax cut for individuals and businesses.

While the specifics on tax cuts and spending cuts have yet to be written, Domenici, a New Mexico Republican, said all sides agreed it will have four basic tax cuts -- a $500 per child credit, a reduction in the capital gains tax rate, an education credit and reductions in inheritance taxes.

The budget blueprint will save over the next five years $78 billion from defence programmes, $61 billion on domestic government, $115 billion from Medicare health care for the elderly, $17 billion from Medicaid and $45 billion from other mandatory programmes such as student loans, federal retirement, housing and sales of broadcast airwaves.

Republican leaders plan to pass the budget by the May 23 date for a Memorial Day holiday break. They aim to pass the spending cuts by July 4. And, although they also want to pass the tax bill by July 4, a Republican congressional aide said August was a more probable deadline.
The budget came under attack from an influential Republican senator who announced he will oppose it.

Texan Phil Gramm charged that most of its savings came from a $225 billion windfall that budget analysts discovered when they examined the impact of the current healthy economy on expected increased tax revenues.
